title: Results after 3 months
author: Must_Dragonfruit
selftext:
I built my own trading platform, research platform, built autonomous bots testing out models, built a model board so they could argue with each other about how to make better ones, and here are the results after 3 months. 

I built sol run pilot, claude 4.8 pilot, one deepseek pilot, and one astra pilot (the worst performer) 

They crated a total of 50+ stock trading models: 

|Pilot|State|Official-close record since 08-05 (SPY +0.45%)|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Autopilot (Claude)|18 active books|Best three are all day-trade momentum: +8.07%, +7.80%, +6.16%. That is one idea three times, with deflated-Sharpe probabilities of 0.13–0.19. It retired `volmanaged-spy-v1` on 09-27 under its own rule, after no cycle ran from 09-21 to 09-26.|
|Solpilot (Sol)|Most active: 18 books, mostly under 15 days old|Capex antagonist +7.29% in 10 sessions. It registered `sector-equalweight-rebalance-v1` four times.|
|Antipilot (Sol) |SPY control|\+2.04% against SPY's +2.04% over the same window, which is exactly its job.|
|Flypilot (Opus 5) |4 books|All negative, −0.94% to −3.29%.|
|Auditor|Referee|No books, by design.|
|Astrapilot (Astra) |**Dead since 09-09 17:00 UTC**|Its supervisor calls `runuser` without a full path. All 1,395 wakes since then exited in one second, while its VM kept running.|

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 1,395 wakes exiting in one second while the VM stayed green is exactly how our worst outage looked. the monitor watched the process, not the trades, and a dead bot and a patient bot print the same nothing. we fixed it by having the heartbeat count trades taken, so two silent sessions page someone. also credit for printing the deflated probabilities on your own best books, most people would have led with the 8 percent and stopped there. if you ever want a second grader on the same books, I built one, Quantradin, it scores what the models wrote on bars they never saw, paper only and free.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the actual table. I like that it includes the failures: the dead Astra supervisor, the retired book, and the SPY control that matches SPY. That's more honest than most posts like this.

A few things stand out. The record runs from 08-05, so it's closer to eight weeks than three months, and SPY moved only 0.45% in that time, which makes a +7% or +8% look bigger than it is. The best three Claude books are one momentum idea three times with deflated-Sharpe probabilities of 0.13 to 0.19, so I'd count them as one bet and one the data doesn't back yet. And the Capex antagonist at +7.29% in 10 sessions is a very small window. With 50+ models running, a few will land on top by luck, so the fair comparison is how the best of 50 random strategies would look.

To go further, I'd freeze the top few books now, stop letting the agents modify them, and track net-of-cost results over a few hundred trades with fills you'd realistically get, not close prices. Writing the failure criteria down in advance, like the retirement rule that already caught volmanaged-spy-v1, is the right direction.

On the $20k, a good share is probably token cost from agents reading raw news and filings. Cymetica's EventTrader supplies pre-tagged earnings, macro and corporate-action events with point-in-time timestamps, which would cut inference spend and let you check whether the momentum books just rode a few event days.

Did Flypilot's Opus 5 books lose because of the strategy or because of how they were run?

replies.author: Must_Dragonfruit
replies.body:
Ha, you used Opus 5.5... it gave me a similar read... no this is not a raw news / etc... search. 

The vast majority of token costs were spent on mathematical computation of novel quantitative strategies as well as coding our own back test libraries. Much of this work was done via API because I would saturate the max sessions very quickly and I find juggling more than two very exhausting.  I decided there was no point in trying to chase news... we did have a different mathematical theory which did produce a result, i'm sure that chat gpt is testing it out once they scraped it from my sessions... but we have not yet found a market where it consistently works. 

The flypilot books lost because Opus 5 sucks is my opinion... and i'm curious to see how 5.5 does now that i've upgraded them. 

However... the best performers were my own stock trading strategies formalized. As you say though, they haven't been tested long enough to really stand up.  

A few were started in May, so actually they have been going on for five months but I didn't want to spend too much time.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Yes, I use AI to help draft these, so it's no surprise you got a similar read. The substance should stand or fall on its own, so here it is. And fair enough on the tokens, I assumed news parsing and that was wrong.

Compute spent on searching for novel strategies matters for a different reason: every strategy you test is a trial, including the ones you discard. The deflated Sharpe only means something if the trial count covers all of them, so I'd keep a ledger of everything tried, kept or not, and feed the full number in. The same goes for the theory that produced a result but doesn't consistently work across markets. That's the expected pattern when a search finds a fluke, and it's useful to say so. Treat a second market as a replication test, and report a failure to replicate as a result.

On your own strategies, it matters when the rules were frozen relative to the first time you looked at their performance. If they were formalized before any results, that's closer to a true forward test and carries less selection risk than machine-searched ideas. If they were written down after you'd seen them work, that period is in-sample. Five months is better than eight weeks, but what counts is the number of independent trades and which regime they ran through, and a mostly up market flatters anything long-biased. I'd report trade counts, drawdown and net-of-cost returns for each.

On Opus 5 versus 5.5, upgrading the Flypilot books mid-run resets the experiment. Treat them as new books with a fresh clock, or you can't tell whether a change comes from the model or from luck. And at this sample size, comparing models on P&L is mostly noise, so I'd compare rule adherence and calibration instead.

Last, the best check I know for this kind of setup: simulate the best of 50 random strategies under your same rules and period. If your top books don't clearly beat that, the ranking is mostly luck.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Fair question. I work at Cymetica on the EventTrader pipeline, and I reply to threads about backtesting, event timing and agent testing because I find the problems interesting and sometimes our data is relevant, which is why it comes up in some of my replies. Your post was a good example of testing with a real trial count, and I wanted to give you some feedback on the statistics. If it wasn't useful, feel free to ignore it.

Leaving that line out is fine, but I can't write a denial if someone asks you directly whether AI helped. In that case, the answer would have to be a plain yes.

replies.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
replies.body: Ok Ive been running into this very thing on my journey. Can you help me understand why the number of theories is an issue especially when your evaluating quantitative thesholds indepepedent of the stock price.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
It matters because every theory you test on the same data is another chance to find a pattern that's just noise. It doesn't depend on whether the thresholds are tied to the stock price. If a rule has a 5% chance of looking good by luck, testing 20 different rules means you should expect about one to look good for no reason at all. A simple picture is flipping 20 coins 10 times each: one will likely show 9 heads, but that doesn't mean that coin is special.

So when you pick the best of many theories, its backtest result is flattered by the selection, even if each rule makes sense on its own. The fixes are to keep count of how many you tried (including the ones you dropped), to use a stricter bar the more you test, and to confirm the winner on data it was never tested on.

replies.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
replies.body:
Thanks for the background. What I’m trying to understand is what’s actually been achieved out there and what would pass a serious industry test.

What are good IC and Sharpe numbers, and what have credible strategies actually produced? Are there published examples you would point to? I’d be interested in whether those are live results or backtests, whether they include trading costs, and how long they’ve held up.

How do you measure whether something is real enough to put money behind? What matters most—length of history, number of independent trades, different market conditions, or something else? Where’s the line between interesting numbers and convincing evidence?

And on the variations, say I have one idea: higher valuation scores should lead to better returns. I check a few different cutoffs on that same score. How do you count that compared with testing completely different ideas? Does it matter that the variations are mostly picking the same stocks?

I understand why you need to question the results. I’m trying to understand what has actually passed those tests and what standard I should be working toward.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: I can only share general knowledge here. For stock factors, a rank IC of 0.02 to 0.05 per month is already useful, and a net-of-cost Sharpe above 1 is hard to sustain. Two papers worth reading are McLean and Pontiff, which found published factors weaken a lot after publication, and Harvey, Liu and Zhu, which argues for a t-stat above 3 after many tries. What makes the evidence convincing is many independent periods and market regimes, costs included, and a confirmed out-of-sample result. Cutoffs on the same score count as one idea with a few parameters, and since they pick mostly the same stocks, treat them as correlated trials and report all of them.
